'''Manhattan Beach''' is a residential neighborhood in the [[New York City]] [[borough (New York City)|borough]] of [[Brooklyn]]. It is bounded by the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the south and east, by [[Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn|Sheepshead Bay]] on the north, and [[Brighton Beach]] to the west. Traditionally known as an [[Italian American|Italian]] and [[Ashkenazi Jews|Ashkenazi Jewish]] neighborhood, it is also home to a sizable community of [[Sephardi Jews]] and a large [[Russian Americans in New York City|Russian Jewish immigrant]] presence.

Manhattan Beach is part of [[Brooklyn Community Board 15|Brooklyn Community District 15]], and its primary [[ZIP Code]] is 11235.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the 61st Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department]].<ref name="NYPD 61st Precinct"/> Politically it is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 48th District. The area is also represented by the Manhattan Beach Community Group, established in 1941, and the Manhattan Beach Neighborhood Association, established in 2008.

==History==
[[File:View of Manhattan Beach Hotel, Coney Island (2786857415).jpg|thumb|left|Manhattan Beach Hotel {{circa|1905}}]]
Manhattan Beach was the most upscale of the three major resort areas that developed at [[Coney Island]] shortly after the [[American Civil War]]; the other two areas were [[Brighton Beach]] and West Brighton.<ref name="heartofconeyisland">{{cite web|access-date=November 19, 2016|website=heartofconeyisland.com|url=http://www.heartofconeyisland.com/manhattan-beach-coney-island-history.html|title=Coney Island History: The Rise and Fall of Corbin's Manhattan Beach Resort|author= Sullivan, David A. }}</ref>

It was developed in the last quarter of the 19th century as a resort by [[Austin Corbin]], later president of the [[Long Island Rail Road]], for whom the street Corbin Place, which marks the boundary between Brighton Beach and Manhattan Beach, was originally named.<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20000304153211/http://www.lirrhistory.com/nymbry.html The New York and Manhattan Beach Railway]}}, LIRR History. Accessed June 4, 2007. ''"Immediately the whole purpose of the new RR was changed from freight to passenger, in order to service Corbin’s proposed line to the site of his immense Manhattan Beach Hotel that was being constructed on the east end of Coney Island."''</ref> Corbin Place has since been renamed to M. Corbin Place, after [[Margaret Corbin]], the hero of the [[American Revolutionary War]], due to Austin Corbin's antisemitism.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-10-02 |title=Corbin Place to become M. Corbin Place • Brooklyn Paper |url=https://www.brooklynpaper.com/corbin-place-to-become-m-corbin-place/ |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=www.brooklynpaper.com |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1877, Corbin built the famous Manhattan Beach Hotel, followed by the even grander Oriental Hotel in 1880.<ref name="heartofconeyisland"/> The Coney Island Jockey Club horse racing track opened nearby at the same time as Corbin's Oriental Hotel; together, these three establishments drew thousands of visitors to Manhattan Beach.<ref name="heartofconeyisland"/> The hotels held daily concerts led by famous conductors such as Conterno, Gilmore, and [[John Philip Sousa]], and hosted elaborate nightly fireworks displays, drawing tens of thousands of visitors on summer nights and making Manhattan Beach a renowned summer seaside resort.<ref name="heartofconeyisland"/> Sousa composed the [[Manhattan Beach (march)|"Manhattan Beach"]] march in 1893 to commemorate the beach resort. Corbin, an [[antisemitism|anti-Semite]] who served as the secretary of the American Society for the Suppression of Jews, barred Jews from the resort.<ref name="marcmatranalostplantations">Marc R. Matrana, [https://books.google.com/books?id=D1YfPjRCucQC&dq=%22abner+johnson%22+kentucky&pg=PA41 ''Lost Plantations of the South''], Oxford, Mississippi: University Press of Mississippi, 2009, pp. 40–43</ref><ref>Leonard Benardo, Jennifer Weiss, [https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/25/opinion/nyregionopinions/25CIbenardo.html?_r=0 Street Cred], ''The New York Times'', February 25, 2007</ref> In 1895, Corbin built a 12,000 capacity third-mile concrete [[Velodrome|cycling track]] behind the hotel at a cost of $30,000.<ref>{{cite magazine|title=Work Aplenty for Ambitious Anklers|date=April 6, 1922|url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nyp.33433107853016;view=1up;seq=35|magazine=Motorcycle and Bicycle Illustrated|location=New York City|publisher=The Cycling Press|volume=18|issue=14|page=29|via=[[HathiTrust]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Cross|first1=Gary|last2=Walton|first2=John K.|title=The Playful Crowd: Pleasure Places in the Twentieth Century|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Kq7jS-Xaea0C&pg=PA51|year=2005|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=978-0-231-50283-2|page=51}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Condensed Cycling Chat|url=https://newspaperarchive.com/sports-clipping-jul-02-1895-1198395/|work=Warren Evening News|date=July 2, 1895|page=2|via=[[NewspaperARCHIVE.com]]}}</ref>

[[File:"Negro recruits at Manhattan Beach Training Station, (NY).", ca. 1941 - ca. 1945 - NARA - 513165.jpg|thumb|African-American recruits at Manhattan Beach Coast Guard Training Station, ca. 1941 - ca. 1945]]
The [[United States Coast Guard|U.S. Coast Guard]] operated a training station at Manhattan Beach during [[World War II]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://dmna.ny.gov/forts/fortsM_P/manhattanBeach.htm |title=Manhattan Beach Coast Guard Training Station |publisher=New York State Division of Military and Naval Affairs |access-date=March 19, 2020}}</ref>

After the deterioration of the hotel industry in the area, the site of the former Manhattan Beach hotel was developed into a residential area and into Manhattan Beach Park by the [[New York City Parks Department]]. Manhattan Beach Park opened to the public in 1955, to alleviate crowding at the neighboring beaches of Coney Island and Brighton Beach, and continues to serve the public today.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/manhattan-beach-park/history|website=New York City Parks Department|title= Manhattan Beach Park History|access-date=January 3, 2017}}</ref> From 1954 to 1959, the neighborhood was home to [[Manhattan Beach Air Force Station]].<ref name=ANL>{{cite web|title=Manhattan Beach Army Housing Units Brooklyn, New York|url=http://apps.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a215951.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150411075453/http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a215951.pdf|url-status=live|archive-date=April 11, 2015|website=Environmental Research Division [[Argonne National Laboratory]]|access-date=April 5, 2015|date=November 1989}}</ref> From the 1980s, Manhattan Beach has become an enclave for higher end middle class [[Russian Jews]].<ref name="nyt1">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/09/16/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-of-living-in-manhattan-beach.html|title=If You're Thinking of Living in: Manhattan Beach|date=September 16, 1990|work=The New York Times}}</ref> The [[Manhattan Beach Jewish Center]] was listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] in 2015.<ref name="nps">{{cite web|url=https://www.nps.gov/subjects/nationalregister/upload/weekly-list-2015-national-register-of-historic-places.pdf|title=National Register of Historic Places Listings: Weekly List of Actions Taken on Properties: 5/26/15 through 5/29/15 |website=National Park Service|date=June 5, 2015}}</ref>

== Demographics ==
According to data from the 2020 United States Census, the population of Manhattan Beach was 4,684.<ref name="NYC_DCP_2020">{{cite web |title=2020 Census Demographic and Housing Characteristics Data |url=https://www.nyc.gov/site/planning/data-maps/nyc-population/2020-census.page |publisher=New York City Department of City Planning |access-date=September 17, 2026}}</ref> 

The neighborhood is predominantly White, comprising roughly 80% of the total population, with smaller populations of Asian (10%) and Hispanic or Latino (4%) residents.<ref name="NYC_DCP_2020" />

Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref><ref>[http://www.latfor.state.ny.us/maps/2012c/CD_nyc.pdf New York City Congressional Districts], New York State Legislative Task Force on Demographic Research and Reapportionment. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref> It is in the [[New York State Senate]]'s 22nd district,<ref>[http://www.latfor.state.ny.us/maps/2012s/SD_map_rep_22.pdf Senate District 22], New York State Legislative Task Force on Demographic Research and Reapportionment. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref><ref>[http://www.latfor.state.ny.us/maps/2012s/SD_nyc.pdf 2012 Senate District Maps: New York City], New York State Legislative Task Force on Demographic Research and Reapportionment. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref><ref>[http://www.latfor.state.ny.us/maps/2012a/AD_nyc.pdf 2012 Assembly District Maps: New York City], New York State Legislative Task Force on Demographic Research and Reapportionment. Accessed November 17, 2018.</ref>  and the [[New York City Council]]'s 48th district.<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/brooklyn.pdf Current City Council Districts for Kings County], [[New York City]]. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref>

==Police and crime==
Manhattan Beach is patrolled by the 61st Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 2575 Coney Island Avenue.<ref name="NYPD 61st Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/61st-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 61st Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref>
The 61st Precinct ranked 5th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/brooklyn/sheepshead-bay/|title=Sheepshead Bay – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=www.dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170415051938/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/brooklyn/sheepshead-bay|archive-date=April 15, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The 61st Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 88.2% between 1990 and 2018. The precinct reported 1 murder, 17 rapes, 150 robberies, 170 felony assaults, 169 burglaries, 584 grand larcenies, and 72 grand larcenies auto in 2018.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-061pct.pdf|title=61st Precinct CompStat Report|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=July 22, 2018}}</ref>

== Fire safety ==
Manhattan Beach is served by the [[New York City Fire Department]] (FDNY)'s Engine Co. 246/Ladder Co. 169, located at 2732 East 11th Street.<ref>{{Cite FDNY locations}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |website=FDNYtrucks.com |title=Engine Company 246/Ladder Company 169 | url=http://www.fdnytrucks.com/files/html/brooklyn/e246.htm | access-date=March 2, 2019}}</ref>

==Education==
===Schools and institutes===
[[File:KBCC Rotunda jeh.jpg|thumb|The Rotunda at [[Kingsborough Community College]]]]
[[FIle:PS195 MB jeh.JPG|thumb|right|PS 195]]
[[Kingsborough Community College]], which is the part of the [[City University of New York]], occupies the entire eastern tip of Manhattan Beach. The college's halls and departments are spread out through the area. [[The Leon M. Goldstein High School for the Sciences]] is located on the campus of Kingsborough Community College.

The [[New York City Department of Education]] operates public schools in the area. Manhattan Beach is zoned to PS 195 Manhattan Beach School<ref>{{cite web |url=https://schools.nyc.gov/SchoolPortals/22/K195/default.htm?searchType=school |title = Find a School - New York City Department of Education}}</ref> for grades K–5 and PS 225, the Eileen E. Zaglin School<ref>{{cite web|url=http://schools.nyc.gov/schoolportals/21/K225|title=Welcome - P.S. K225 - The Eileen E. Zaglin - K225 - New York City Department of Education|website=schools.nyc.gov}}</ref> for grades pre school– middle school. In 1992, special education school PS 771K was opened at this building.{{Citation needed|date=November 2010}}

Private schools in the area include Mazel Day School, a [[Jewish day school]] for grades K–8 with a preschool in [[Brighton Beach]], and the Yeshiva Gedolah Bais Shimon of Manhattan Beach, which is a post-high school rabbinical program.

===Library===
While there is no location of the [[Brooklyn Public Library]] in Manhattan Beach, the Sheepshead Bay branch nearby is located at 2636 East 14th Street, near Avenue Z.<ref>{{cite web | title=Sheepshead Bay Library | website=Brooklyn Public Library | date=August 22, 2011 | url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/sheepshead-bay | access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref>

==Transportation==

=== Public transportation ===
Manhattan Beach is served by [[MTA Regional Bus Operations]]' {{NYC bus link|B1|B49|prose=y}} bus routes. Both operate along Oriental Boulevard to/from [[Kingsborough Community College]]. A stop at Emmons Avenue/Shore Boulevard at the border with [[Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn|Sheepshead Bay]] is used by the {{NYC bus link|BM3}}, while eastbound {{NYC bus link|B4}} buses bypass without stopping.<ref>{{cite NYC bus map|B}}</ref>

=== Roads ===
[[File:Одна из немногих многоэтажек.jpg|thumb|right|Buildings in the neighborhood]]
The community's street names, derived from England, are in alphabetical order from A to P. From west to east, they are named Amherst, Beaumont, Coleridge, Dover, Exeter, Falmouth, Girard, Hastings, Irwin, Jaffray, Kensington, Langham, Mackenzie, Norfolk, Oxford, and Pembroke; the names Quentin and Reynolds exist on old maps. The A-P streets are interrupted by the two-way Ocean Avenue between Exeter and Falmouth. They are bounded by Shore Boulevard and Oriental Boulevard on the north and south sides and West End Avenue on the western bottom, and are partially intersected by Hampton Avenue.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://forgotten-ny.com/2013/07/kingsborough-community-college-manhattan-beach/|title=KINGSBOROUGH COMMUNITY COLLEGE, Manhattan Beach|last=Walsh|first=Kevin|date=2013-07-18|website=Forgotten New York|language=en-US|access-date=2020-03-18}}</ref>

[[File:MB Beach jeh.jpg|left|thumb|The beach, 2009.]]
Corbin Place was originally named for [[Austin Corbin]], the original developer of Manhattan Beach; in 2007, it was renamed M. Corbin Place for American Revolutionary War patriot [[Margaret Corbin]]. Austin Corbin had restricted Jewish guests at his hotel and enacted restrictive covenants to prevent Jews from buying real estate in the area. After Austin Corbin's death the policy was canceled and the neighborhood attracted a large number of Jewish residents.<ref name="Romano 2007">{{cite web | last=Romano | first=Denise | title=A new namesake for Corbin Place | website=New York Daily News | date=2007-04-05 | url=https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/brooklyn/new-namesake-corbin-place-article-1.207756 | access-date=2021-07-10}}</ref>
